text: To amass something is to gather a large amount of it, a bit at a time, over a long stretch. The word suggests a pile that keeps growing, so you amass a collection rather than a single object. Jim Irsay spent his whole life amassing rock memorabilia, adding one piece after another.

A cache is a group of things stored away together in one place, often hidden. You may know the word from video games, where a supply cache is a stash of gear waiting to be found, and that is the original meaning too. Here archaeologists found a cache of coloured pebbles that someone had tucked away in a cave 300,000 years ago.

Something enduring lasts a long time without fading away. It comes from the verb endure, to keep going through hard times, so an enduring thing has already proved it can last. Coins, comics, sports cards and memorabilia are called enduring because people have wanted them for decades.

When something is gathering dust, nobody has touched it for so long that dust has settled on it. People use it for anything forgotten and unused, like a bike gathering dust in the garage. The headline asks whether a forgotten box in your attic might actually be worth a fortune.

Memorabilia are objects kept because of the person or event they are connected to, not because they are useful. A jersey a player actually wore, or a drum a famous drummer played, counts as memorabilia. The word shares a root with memory.

Collectibles are ordinary objects that people collect and trade, and that become valuable because collectors want them. Cards, coins, stamps and comics are the classic examples. How big that market has grown is the subject of this whole article.

A hearth is the floor of a fireplace, the spot where a fire is actually built. Before stoves existed, the hearth was where all the cooking happened, so the word also came to stand for home itself. The cave near Tel Aviv holds the oldest hearth anyone has found.

Archaeologists are scientists who work out how people lived long ago by digging up what they left behind. They study bones, tools, pots and buildings rather than written records. In this cave they found animal bones and tools from 300,000 years ago.

Primitive means belonging to a very early stage, before things became advanced. A primitive tool is a simple one, like a sharpened stone rather than a metal blade. It describes how early and basic something is, not how badly it was made.

Startling means surprising enough to make you stop short. It is stronger than merely interesting, and it comes from startle, to give someone a sudden shock. The bones and tools were ordinary, but a pile of pretty pebbles nobody had used was startling.

Aesthetic has to do with how something looks and whether it is beautiful. If an object's value is aesthetic, it is worth something because it is pleasing to look at, not because it does a job. The Stone Age pebbles could not cut or dig anything, so their value was purely aesthetic.

Tel Aviv is a large city on the coast of Israel. The cave in this story sits just east of it and was uncovered in 2000 while a road was being built. Finds like that often turn up by accident during building work.

The Stone Age is the long stretch of human history when tools were made from stone, wood and bone, before metal was used. It lasted hundreds of thousands of years. The pebbles were too small to have done any Stone Age job.

An impulse is a sudden urge to do something that arrives before you have thought it through. Grabbing a snack you had not planned to eat is acting on impulse. A Yale professor thinks the impulse to collect is very old and may be built into us.

Something ingrained is fixed so deeply that it is hard to remove. The picture behind the word is a stain worked right into the grain of wood. Calling the urge to collect ingrained means it is part of how people are, not a habit we recently picked up.

An obsessive is someone who cannot stop thinking about one particular thing. Here it means collectors who will chase a single missing card or coin for years. The word is half a joke, but it points at real single-mindedness.

A specialist knows one narrow subject extremely well instead of knowing a little about many things. A specialist dealer might handle nothing but old coins. That deep knowledge is exactly what once gave dealers the upper hand over ordinary buyers.

A dealer buys things and then sells them on for a profit. Because a dealer owns the stock, they have to pay little and charge more to make money. The article keeps contrasting dealers with auction houses, which never own what they sell.

To get in on the action is to join something exciting or profitable that is already happening. It carries a hint of not wanting to be left out. The big auction houses saw how much money collectibles were making and wanted a share.

An auction house is a company that runs sales where buyers bid against each other and the highest offer wins. Christie's, Sotheby's and Heritage Auctions are all auction houses. They usually do not own what they sell; they run the sale and keep a share of the price.

Christie's is one of the two most famous auction houses in the world, founded in London in 1766. It made $6.2bn in sales in 2025. It built its name on fine art and has only recently moved into collectibles.
Sotheby's is the other giant auction house, founded in 1744 and even older than Christie's. It took $7bn in 2025. Its weekly sales of basketball jerseys show how far it has moved into collectibles.

Late placed in front of a person's name means that person has died. So a late American sports-team owner is one who is no longer alive, not one who turned up after the start. It is a gentle, formal way of saying dead.

An auctioneer is the person, or the company, that runs an auction. They call out the rising offers and decide the moment the bidding has stopped. Heritage is described here as the most important collectibles auctioneer.

Heritage Auctions is the auction house this article follows. It began in 1976 as a small coin dealer sharing an office in Dallas and now has 900 employees. Last year it sold $2.16bn worth of collectibles.

A market maker is a business so large that the prices it charges become the prices everyone else uses. Because so many sales pass through it, the rest of the market follows its lead. Heritage has become a market maker in collectibles.
A firm is simply a company or business. This has nothing to do with firm meaning hard or steady. Writers use it so they do not have to repeat the company's name every sentence.

The Belgian Congo was a colony in central Africa ruled by Belgium from 1908 until 1960. Today that country is the Democratic Republic of Congo. Because the old country no longer exists, its banknotes are exactly the kind of thing collectors hunt for.

Eye-watering means so extreme that it almost makes your eyes sting. It is used mostly about prices, and always means shockingly high. A pair of shoes from a 1939 film sold for $32.5m, which is an eye-watering sum.

A benefit auction is one held to raise money for a cause rather than for the seller's own pocket. The seller gives the proceeds away. Dmitry Muratov sold his Nobel medal at one, and it reached $103.5m.

A Nobel prize is one of the highest honours in the world, given each year for work in science, literature and peace, and the winner receives a gold medal. Dmitry Muratov is a Russian journalist who won one. He put his medal up at a charity auction.

Items made in multiples are produced in many identical copies rather than as one of a kind. Baseball cards and coins are made in multiples; a painting is not. That is why Steve Ivy says you cannot collect a set of art.

To validate something is to confirm that it really has the worth it claims. Art is institutionally validated, meaning museums and experts are the ones who confirm its value. Collectibles are community validated, meaning ordinary collectors do it instead.

An asset is anything you own that has value, and an asset class is a whole family of them, such as shares, houses or gold. Treating collectibles as an asset class means investors now think about cards and coins the way they think about shares. That is a fairly recent change.

A speculator buys something hoping its price will rise so they can sell it for more, with no interest in keeping it. That is the opposite of a collector, who buys what they love. Both kinds of buyer are in this market at once.

To diversify is to spread your money across different kinds of things so one bad result cannot wipe you out. If shares fall, old coins might hold their value. It is the money version of not putting all your eggs in one basket.

A convention here is a big gathering of people who share one interest, with stalls, displays and trading. This is not the other meaning of convention, a custom or tradition. A stamp convention is a hall full of people buying and swapping stamps.

To incorporate a business is to register it officially as a company with a legal identity of its own. Before 1982 Steve Ivy and his partner were two people trading; afterwards they were Heritage Auctions. It marks the point where a business becomes formal.

To credit something for a result is to say that is what caused it. Mr Ivy credits early online sales for his success, meaning he believes that is why the firm grew. It is a different meaning from credit as money you borrow.

Adoption here means taking something up and starting to use it. Early adoption of online sales means Heritage started using the internet before its rivals did. It has nothing to do with adopting a child.
An operation here means a business, usually a small one. A two- or three-man operation is a company with only two or three people in it. It is not a medical operation or a military one.

Expertise is deep skill and knowledge in one area, built up over years. The little firms Heritage bought had expertise but no way to reach many customers. Buying the firm was really a way of buying the people who knew things.

To subsume one thing into another is to absorb it until it no longer exists separately. When Heritage subsumed a small dealer, the dealer's name disappeared and its experts became Heritage's experts. The larger thing swallows the smaller one.

Something done in-house is done by a company's own staff rather than by outsiders. Bringing a small firm in-house means turning its people into your own employees. The opposite is paying someone outside to do the work.

An information advantage is knowing something important in a deal that the other person does not. Dealers knew what coins had cost them and what similar coins had sold for, and buyers knew neither, so dealers could steer the price. Published online prices are what took that advantage away.
To be in the dark about something is to have no information about it. Nobody is necessarily lying to you; you simply cannot see. Buyers were in the dark about what items had really been selling for.

On both fronts means in both of the areas being talked about. A front was originally the line where an army fights, so trouble on two fronts meant trouble in two places at once. Buyers lacked information on both fronts: what dealers paid, and what dealers charged.

An edge here is an advantage over the people you are competing with. It has nothing to do with the edge of a table. If you know the going price of a card and the other person does not, you have an edge.

When goods are consigned, the owner hands them to someone else to sell but still owns them until they sell. The seller takes a share of the final price rather than buying the item outright. Most of what Heritage auctions is consigned.

To take a cut is to keep a share of the money from a deal you helped make, usually a percentage of the total. Auction houses take a cut of every sale instead of owning the goods. Sell for more, and their cut is bigger too.

Buy low and sell high is the basic rule for making money by trading: pay little, then charge more. It sounds simple and is actually hard, because you have to judge what a thing is really worth before you pay. An auction house sidesteps the problem by never buying at all.
A fad is something that becomes wildly popular very fast and then fades just as fast. Fidget spinners were a fad. The article sets fads against the big four, whose popularity has lasted decades.
To dissipate is to scatter and fade until nothing is left. Smoke dissipates in the air, and so does a craze. Fads bubble up and dissipate while the big four stay put.

Muscle cars are powerful American cars with very large engines, built mostly in the 1960s and 70s. They were bought up by people who had wanted them as teenagers. Now that those buyers are old, prices have fallen.
To have a good run is to enjoy a stretch of success that then comes to an end. It comes from sport, where a run is a string of wins. Muscle cars had a good run before their prices declined.

Disposable income is the money you have left after paying for the things you must have, like rent and food. It is the money you could spend on anything at all, or on nothing. Collectors in their late 30s finally have some, which is part of why old cards have become expensive.

Nostalgia is a warm, slightly sad longing for a time in your past. It makes people want the exact objects from their childhood back again. Adults who collected cards at nine now pay a lot to own those same cards.
When something sets in, it arrives and then stays rather than passing through. Winter sets in; so does nostalgia. The phrase is used for conditions that settle over you and do not lift.

Whopping means strikingly large, and it always sounds informal and a little amazed. Calling $16.5m a whopping price is the writer telling you to find it ridiculous. You would not use the word in a formal report.

Pokemon is a Japanese game and cartoon series that appeared in the mid-1990s, with collectible cards showing its creatures. The children who collected them then are now in their late 30s and early 40s. One rare card recently sold for $16.5m.

Cultural assets are valuable things people own for what they mean rather than what they do, such as art, memorabilia and rare objects. Calling art and collectibles one broader system means they are no longer two separate markets. Plenty of people now buy from both.

To augur something is to be a sign that it is on the way. An augur in ancient Rome was a priest who looked for omens in the flight of birds. Saying this augurs a healthy future means it points towards one.

An enthusiast is someone with a strong, cheerful interest in something. Enthusiasts keep buying even in bad times, because they buy for love rather than profit. The word comes from a Greek root meaning inspired.

The financial crisis of 2007-09 was a worldwide economic collapse that started with bad housing loans in America. Banks failed and millions of people lost their jobs. Heritage still did well, because hard times push people to sell what they own.

Something all-consuming takes up all of your attention and leaves room for nothing else. A hobby that becomes all-consuming has stopped being just a hobby. The picture behind the word is a fire that burns everything in its path.

A compulsion is an urge you feel you have to act on, even when you know it is not sensible. It is much stronger than simply wanting something. Mr Ivy jokes that collecting is a compulsion to complete a set.
